q: Seen so many negative induction stories, was terrified because of them
cx: Told at 39 weeks she must be induced; the negative induction stories she had read terrified her.

q: I did end up requesting epidural at 8CM dilated, more to do with getting tired rather than the pain
cx: After an induction she asked for an epidural late, out of tiredness rather than pain.

q: I was worried about getting induced and being restricted to the bed and “inevitably” getting the epidural, but in the end I had my daughter 10 hours after starting my induction, and 4 hours after labor *really* started, and being flexible about my birth plan was very helpful.
cx: From her hospital bed, a first-time mother says her fear of induction didn't come true and flexibility helped.
r: medication: epidural; induction outcome, not a promise

q: I didn’t have any of the negative feelings I thought I’d have about getting the epidural, and everyone told me “good job” :)
cx: Had planned no epidural; after getting one she felt none of the expected guilt.

q: At this point, my goal of going without the epidural went out the window as I thought “I would survive this without pain meds, but fuck that”.
cx: Once contractions came fast after her waters were broken, she dropped the no-epidural goal.

q: During my pregnancy, I found reading post on this sub of the wide variety of birth experiences really useful.
cx: UK mother says reading varied birth stories during pregnancy helped her prepare.

q: Everything I’ve read online says it should last 48 hours max, so we were very confused, but at my two prearranged membrane sweeps the midwives weren’t concerned at all (even as I had contractions in front of them 😭)
cx: Five days of early-labour contractions didn't match what she read online; midwives were unconcerned.

q: Really panicky, terrified that I was so exhausted I’d wouldn’t get through active labour, and had no idea how much longer I’d have to wait without hospital pain management, since the hospital guidelines say to ring them only once you’ve hit 3-4 contractions within 10 minutes.
cx: After nights without sleep in early labour, she feared she couldn't cope and felt bound by the call-in rule.

q: My husband insisted that we call the maternity unit to see if they could do anything.
cx: Her husband pushed them to ring the unit before the official timing rule was met.

q: I was worried they would think I was ridiculous for being there, but no, they were wonderful and I felt completely cared for.
cx: She feared midwives would think her silly for coming in early; they made her feel cared for.

q: So my advice is to remember that every birth is different, and you need to listen carefully to your gut about when to bend the rules. If you are ever unsure, just ring your maternity unit!
cx: Her takeaway after a long early labour: trust your gut over the timing rule and ring the unit.

q: I’m afraid of resenting the baby of what I had to let go in order to have it, I’m afraid of being impatient and emotionally unavailable. Im afraid I don’t have enough.
cx: Quoting her own post from just after a positive test, she feared resenting the baby and losing her life.

q: I got quite a few comments about how I was not ready and why I am even having a kid if I don’t like them in general.
cx: Strangers told her she wasn't ready when she shared doubts early in pregnancy.

q: So if anyone’s spiraling and going through the same feelings, all I can say is : IT’S NORMAL, it’s such a huge step and change, but the final destination is just amazing
cx: Five months postpartum she tells doubting pregnant women the fear was normal and it turned out well.

q: your husband/boyfriend has to be as involved and aware of everything as you, not as just an executive waiting for instructions for it to work.
cx: Says getting her old life back depends on a partner who knows everything, not one awaiting instructions.

q: I had a difficult birth but 2 weeks later I had already forgotten how hard it’s been.
cx: Reassuring a pregnant commenter that hard moments fade fast.

q: I was hooked up to a monitor and not told what would be happening. Eventually we queried and were told I was waiting for a bed to be free on the labour ward (understandable but it would’ve been nice to know!).
cx: Admitted for induction in the UK, she waited without being told why: no bed on the labour ward.

q: I had been handling the contractions well with the tens machine (definitely recommend!!)
cx: During an induction she found the TENS machine helped with contractions.

q: If you have a c section have your birth partner make note of the time and push for the staff to help you move as soon as that time passes. If you’re feeding, call them back as soon as you’re done.
cx: Staff were hours late getting her moving after the caesarean; she says the birth partner should chase it.

q: Later on I had to press the call button as I couldn’t bear the pain anymore and I was asked “when did you last have painkillers?” And I thought isn’t that your job?!
cx: After her caesarean, staff asked her when she'd last had pain relief; she assumed they were tracking it.

q: I was quite emotional as I’d spent some time believing I was meeting my baby at 39 weeks.
cx: Decided against a planned induction after talking with her midwife and felt emotional losing the date.

q: I snapped at the nurses and my boyfriend who apologized for my snapping. They brushed it off because they understood.
cx: During pushing she snapped at everyone; her boyfriend apologised for her and staff understood.

q: My boyfriend helped me hold her cause I was shaky and not exactly sober. He kissed me and was so proud of me. My grandparents and mom were crying because she was beautiful and they were proud of me.
cx: Right after the birth her boyfriend and family were in the room, proud of her.

q: Throughout pregnancy I had panic attacks when I thought about birth. I was utterly terrified. My biggest fear was the pain and how would I be able to cope with it. The fear made it difficult to function sometimes as it was all I could think about.
cx: Looking back on a pregnancy dominated by fear of birth pain.

q: In the second trimester I came up with my birth plan which helped a bit with the fear. […] Many people told me just to get an epidural but I had many fears around that as well and decided that was something I really didn't want.
cx: Writing a birth plan eased her fear a little; people kept telling her to just get an epidural.
r: mental health: fear of birth; epidural

q: I thought to myself "if I'm feeling like this now then how will I cope with the later stages."
cx: In the birth unit she doubted she could cope, assuming labour had far to go.

q: I am incredibly proud of myself as I was so terrified before but I managed to cope and it was nowhere near as scary or painful as people made out. I didn't even need to use some of the things I had brought with me (birth comb and sensory box).
cx: After a feared birth she felt proud; some items she packed, a birth comb and sensory box, went unused.
r: mental health: fear of birth (tokophobia context)

q: She told me not to get excited since it was my first birth. I got a cervical check and was 10cm
cx: When she said she felt the urge to push, the nurse said not to get excited as it was her first.

q: The second she touched my chest all I could do was cry. Every ache, every pain, every sleepless night, just so worth it.
cx: First-time mother on the moment her baby was placed on her chest.

q: Like many of you, I did a lot of birth preparation and hypnobirthing prep. I knew all about ventouse and forceps, but in the thick of a very long labour, I was introduced to something called the Odon Assist which I'd never heard of.
cx: Despite much birth and hypnobirthing preparation, she met an assisted-delivery option she had never heard of.
r: unit mentions past loss in a reply; medical device

q: Because the hospital was at complete capacity, there was a massive 56-hour backlog between my rods being removed on Monday morning and finally getting a bed on the delivery suite to have my waters broken on Wednesday. All in all I was on the induction ward for 5 nights.
cx: UK induction delayed by a full hospital: five nights on the induction ward.
r: unit mentions past loss in a reply; medical condition named in the post

q: because the team coached me through exactly what to expect, I felt safe and empowered.
cx: During an assisted delivery the team's explanation made her feel safe.
r: unit mentions past loss in a reply

q: I think it's really good to do your homework, but I really believe that the most important thing is to feel emotionally supported and having trust in the team around you is paramount.
cx: Advising someone choosing between hospitals: research helps, but trust in the team matters most.
r: unit mentions past loss in a reply

q: i think i feel guilty, like they’re trying to make me feel bad about wanting one for mental health distress - but it might just be my own perception.
cx: After asking her OB practice to record an induction conversation, their reply left her feeling guilty.

q: my husband usually goes with me but couldn’t this one time due to low staff at work! he’s definitely my best advocate. we discussed it and agreed he should be there with me from here on out due to this experience
cx: After a bad appointment alone, she and her husband agree he will attend every visit.
r: unit centred on mental health distress
